The amounts are this utility’s charge codes, not typed. A code carries the price, the basis it multiplies by and the words
the customer reads.
A line is waived, never removed. Waiving needs a reason and records it against your name, and the line stays on the
quote showing $0.00 — so a customer who was not charged and a customer who was never quoted do not look the same
six months later.

Needs a reason, and the lines stay on the quote at $0.00.
Outstanding is a figure, not a state to choose. It is the quote less what was
taken, so it falls out of the two panels on the left rather than being set anywhere.
Nothing outstanding stops this job. The swap is raised, booked and done
whether or not the $35.00 has been paid.
What this does NOT do
Raise an invoice No
Post a journal line No
Touch the account balance No
Appear on the next bill No
It is accepted and marked as cash, and finance reconciles it. That is a
deliberate split: this screen records what was handed over the counter, and the
books are somebody else’s job.
NONE OF THIS EXISTS ON A JOB YET
A work order carries no price today — no lines, no collected figure, no
outstanding. This step is drawn on the fee model the service request already
has, which is ruled and built, rather than as a second and different one.

This one was asked for through the portal, and the portal will not tell them it was booked. Three of the four rows have no template and the fourth is a draft nobody has published — so a customer who asked
online watches nothing happen and rings on Wednesday to ask.
SEND WHAT IT SAYS TO CHANNEL TEMPLATE WHEN
☐ That we have it, and when we will do it Ferraro, L. Email — none exists On raising

Choosing a template
Search templates
⚲  service
Searches the name a human gave it.
TEMPLATE GROUP CHANNEL VARIANT VERSION
Visit booked SMS SMS Default · English v1 Draft
— nothing else matches service — — — —
Everything here is queued, and nothing is sent. This product writes a row per message and no sender picks it up — no email, no text, no print file.
The one template that exists is a draft, and a draft cannot be picked. It is listed rather than hidden, because hiding it sends a clerk looking for something they can see exists — and offering it would queue a
message nobody has approved.
The last row is the one worth arguing about. Telling a customer their bin got smaller and their bill did not is honest and nobody wants to send it.
Print is the floor. Paperless and text reminders are channels on top of the paper, not instead of it, so an account with paperless on gets the email AND the envelope.

list: the machinery still exists and is still how it works, and nobody has to meet it
to add one more kind of complaint.

Three today, and a utility adds what it sells. A hydrant meter hire, a bulk collection, a temporary supply, a meter test — all of them belong here and none of them is in the list yet.
Retire, never delete. A kind that is in use stays readable on every job already logged against it; retiring it only stops it being offered on the form.
This screen is a narrow door onto a bigger list. Underneath, these are two headings of the work catalogue that also holds meter maintenance, readings and connections — with parents, response times and
everything else.
Four ways a customer comes to exist: somebody walks in and asks (a request), a
builder connects an address (a new connect), a clerk types one in (S18), or the
next occupant takes a unit somebody just left (a move-in).
How these fifteen entries differ from the two above
Screens 01 and 02 carry the full treatment — the whole spec table, the data flow and a field table per field. Screens 03 to 17 are drawn and carry the rows that discriminate —
the audited doors, the primary, the write surfaces, the states and the walked row — but their field tables are rolled up into appendix I rather than repeated per screen. That is a
deliberate scoping, stated here rather than left for a reader to notice.
Every drawing in this document is the desktop screen at 1280. The phone drawings were cut on the product owner's instruction. Where a decision only becomes visible when
space is scarce — the KPI strip stacking, the seven-glyph rail wrapping, an eight-column table at 390 — this document no longer shows it, and that is a real gap rather than a tidy-
up: most of these screens are used on a desk, but the move-out and disconnect wizards are the two a person runs standing up.
And every STEP of every flow is drawn as a full screen, not one representative step per wizard. A wizard is not one screen — the new connect is nine, the move-out and the
new account are six each — and an audit that draws step 5 and lists the other eight has audited a ninth of it. 61 production wireframes: 56 flow screens, the two register screens,
and the three remedies.
These are drawn in the product's own UI, read out of its stylesheets rather than approximated. The palette, the type and the geometry come from src/styles/tokens.css; the
shell from AppShell.css (a 240px inverted ink sidebar, an accent fill on the active module, a 56px topbar with a 2px rule); the header from PageHeader.css; the KPI band from
KPIStrip.css; the step rail and its square badges from WizardFrame.tsx; the buttons from buttonKit.ts; the pill from StateFrame.css; the field from FormModal.css; the table from
DataTable.css. Every corner is square because tokens.css sets all three radii to 0 and says so in words.
Required fields carry the asterisk UI-RULES 10 asks for; a dashed block is a stated absence naming the rule it waits on; a disabled control is drawn disabled. The caption under each
screen gives its address and, on the last step of a flow, the endpoint the commit reaches.
The rules this screen is drawn to
Written here because a drawing shows one state and a clerk meets six. Every cell
below was read off the running product — one account opened per status, on
2026-09-10 — and not inferred from the gate code. Where the tenant has no
account in a status, the row says so.
Rule 1 · Every action stays on the screen, in every status
PO ruling 2026-09-10: "keep all buttons on screen" and "keep all icon only disable them". So nothing is hidden by state, and BR-SHL-025 stands unchanged — "a control this role
or this deployment cannot honour renders disabled with its reason, never hidden". No supersession was needed and none is claimed. A control a clerk cannot use still tells them it
exists and why, which is what turns a dead button into an explanation.
The cost is real and is accepted, not hidden: on four of the five statuses that could be tested, four of the six actions are disabled at once, and on pending_activation nine of
the thirteen controls on this screen are disabled together. That is the price of the rule, and the answer to it is the reason text, not removal.

Reading it. Adjust is disabled in every status and that is not a state gate —
"Adjustments are billing rows, and billing is not built. There is no endpoint to post
one to." It is a build gap, so BR-SHL-025 applies to it squarely. Record payment is
live in every status by ruling: BR-PAY-036 — accepting money never changes an
account's status, and gating a closed account out of it would refuse a cheque
that settles a final bill.
A defect this table found: Close out is live on a draft account
The gate is !(isOccupyingAccount || isClosedAccount) (AccountDetailPage.tsx:524–530). A pending_activation account is neither — its behaviour class is non_billable and it is
not terminal — so it falls through the gate and the control renders live. Confirmed on screen on A-12048.
BR-CUS-430 says close-out is for an account whose service has been CUT. A draft never took service. The rule the gate is written from names disconnected, and the tenant has
no disconnected account, so the one status this control exists to serve is the one status that could not be tested. Both halves are the finding.
Rule 2 · All seven rail icons render in every status
Six of the seven are genuinely wired and gate on state, not on a build gap — Print bill and Issue credit go live the moment a bill exists, which is why they are live on the closed
account below and nowhere else. Only Send statement is permanently dead: nothing in this product renders a statement.

Rule 3 · The header carries every fact, and the service chips are what must be managed
PO ruling 2026-09-10: "i will keep all header info and manage it". So no fact leaves the header. What needs a rule is the one part of it that grows without a ceiling: a tenant may
enable eleven services (Electric, Water, Gas, Sewer, Trash, Storm water, Solar, Broadband, Thermal/Heat, Battery, Fire) and each renders a chip.
Measured on the running header by cloning chips into it: 256px at two services, 302px by six, and it keeps climbing. The chip row is 739px wide and a real chip (ELECTRIC · E-
5000) is ~130px, so eleven need ~1,430px — three rows. At that point the tabs and the whole money band are pushed toward the fold on the screen a clerk opens twenty times a
day. The reporter's own production tenant already wraps to two rows at six services.
The rule, and it is a UI-RULES matter rather than a preference: service chips occupy one row. What does not fit collapses into a single + N more chip that expands in place. The
header's height is therefore fixed by its fields and never by its data — which is the same principle the search bar needed (a control must not change size because of what is
header s height is therefore fixed by its fields and never by its data  which is the same principle the search bar needed (a control must not change size because of what is
written in it), and the reason it is stated as a rule rather than fixed once on this screen.
Rule 4 · Everything the API serves is on the screen
PO ruling 2026-09-10: "we should have all these details captured on screen". The account endpoint serves 69 fields. Eleven were served and drawn nowhere, each confirmed absent
by searching the rendered text for its served value:
ageing_segment · ageing_days_past_due · ageing_source · last_bill_at · autopay · status_behavior_class · kind · master_account · balance_basis · balance_source · unit_plan.code
· service_agreements[].started_on.
Ageing is the one that matters and it is proved, not argued. The accounts LIST shows an Ageing column. The DETAIL showed nothing: on A-11812 the API serves
ageing_segment: "d61_90", 61 days past due, source opening_buckets, and the words "past due" appear nowhere on that account's screen. A clerk drills into the account and loses
the single fact that says how overdue it is. It is now the second tile in the band.
Rule 5 · Every fact sits under a named group
PO ruling 2026-09-10: "when we do information architecture, we have to logically group the information, give group a heading so that it is easy for user to understand". Six groups,
and the test is that a new field's group can be named without asking: Money · Service · History · Customer · Billing preferences · Account setup · Portal access.
What grouping removed. The name appeared three times on the old screen, the account number twice, the deposit twice and "Deposit received" twice. Each appears once now.
⚠  The address was the opposite problem and is the more dangerous one: the service address and the mailing address are two DIFFERENT facts that happened to be identical
on the sample account, drawn twice with nothing to tell them apart. A clerk learns to skip the second and then misses it on the landlord account where the bill goes somewhere
else. They are labelled distinctly now, and the mailing address states its absence rather than repeating the service address.
⚠  The service address is marked by an icon, and that puts weight on the icon. It is the same glyph the sidebar uses for Premises, because the service address IS the premises —
and it saves the header a whole text label, which is what the header needed. But an icon with no accessible name is a picture, not a label, and this one is now the only thing
separating the service address from the mailing address. It therefore carries title and aria-label of "Service address", and the mailing address keeps its full text heading rather
than a matching glyph — two similar icons would rebuild the confusion this rule exists to remove.
Rule 6 · No rule id and no database column ever reaches a clerk
B14 rule 32 — "no rule id or internal code in clerk-facing copy" — with rule 31 behind it, "no database id is ever the visible value of a field". Reported from this document's own
drawing: "You are showing DB column — last_bill_at is null…".
⚠  It was the DOCUMENT breaking the rule, not the product. Five live screens were searched in their rendered text — the accounts list, two account details, the new-account
wizard and move-out. Rule ids on screen: none, on all five. Yet the drawings carried nine, because the blueprint's own vocabulary had been written into a clerk's mouth: "No
column at all — BR-CUS-057", "A computed cache with no computer yet — BR-CUS-058", and seven more. Every one is gone; a re-scan of all 61 drawings now returns zero.
The absence sentences say the same thing in a clerk's language. "No column at all — BR-CUS-057. Never $0.00." became "Deposit interest is not tracked, so this is blank rather
than zero." The fact did not move; only the audience did. The rule id belongs in this document's annotations, where a reader is looking one up, and never inside the drawn screen.
Two things are kept on purpose. The import mapping step still shows CUST_NO → customer_no and ACCT → account_no — there the field names ARE the content, because a clerk is
mapping their columns onto ours. And the account Sub-type still reads small_commercial, for the reason below.
A rule-31 finding in the product itself: the account sub-type is a raw enum
The one internal string that does reach a clerk on the live product is the account sub-type. Read off the running screen: single_family on AC-2026-00001 and small_commercial on
A-11812 — underscore, lower case, straight out of the column.
